commit.message:
docs(case-study): record the green CI run on the widened matrix

Ten jobs across Ubuntu and macOS with Node.js 20/22/24, Bun and Deno,
all passing on the pushed branch head.

docs(case-study): record the backward-compatibility measurements

Answers the review request on PR 51 with measurements rather than
expectations: the resolver is compared against main's hardcoded table for
all 25 previously hardcoded specifiers, bare and node:-prefixed, on five
Node.js versions (0 differences each) and on Bun and Deno, where every
difference is inside the fs/promises override.

Two of those Deno differences were regressions from the first dynamic
draft — stat and truncate lost their AsyncFunction wrapper because a
callback API may declare fewer parameters than it accepts — and the
arity clamp that fixed them is now recorded with the before/after logs.

Also records the full-suite runs on Node.js 20/22/24, Bun and Deno, the
main baseline they are compared against, and the CHANGELOG entries for
the clamp, the network-imports skip and the widened CI matrix.

ci: run the suite on every Node.js line the library supports

Which modules are built in is now the runtime's answer rather than a table
inside use-m, so each Node.js line is part of the contract and CI covered only
one of them. The test job matrix now runs Node.js 20.x, 22.x and 24.x; Bun and
Deno bring their own runtime and stay pinned to a single Node.js for `npm ci`,
so the matrix grows by four jobs instead of twelve.

`--experimental-network-imports` was removed in Node.js 22, which made
`tests/network-imports.*` fail on the newer lines for a reason unrelated to
what they test. They now probe for the flag and skip only when Node.js itself
rejects the option; any other failure still fails the test.

`experiments/verify-node-lts.sh` runs the built-in suites and the
backward-compatibility experiment under several Node.js binaries locally.

test(builtins): pin the contract of every previously hardcoded built-in

Issue #50 replaced the `supportedBuiltins` table with runtime discovery, so the
25 specifiers that table used to serve are now answered by a generic loader.
The new suite states what those specifiers have to keep doing - documented
exports, the builtin resolver claiming them instead of handing them to npm, the
runtime's own named exports and default export surviving the loader, the
historical `events`/`stream`/`assert` defaults, the `process` properties the
removed Deno branch copied by hand, and bare and `node:`-prefixed specifiers
resolving alike - and runs on Node.js, Bun and Deno.

`experiments/builtin-backward-compatibility.mjs` measures the same set against
main's entry file, so a difference is reported rather than assumed. It reports
0 differences on Node.js 18, 20, 22, 24 and 26.

fix(builtins): keep every rebuilt fs/promises entry an async function

The rebuild picks a wrapper by the arity derived from the runtime's callback
API, and fell back to the bare `promisify` result when no wrapper matched that
arity. A callback API may declare fewer parameters than it accepts when the
middle ones have defaults - `fs.stat.length` is 1 on Deno and on Node - so the
derived arity was 0 and the fallback applied: on Deno `fs/promises.stat` and
`.truncate` came back as plain functions of length 0, where the hardcoded table
returned async functions of length 2.

The derived arity is now clamped into the range the wrappers cover, so a
rebuilt entry is always an AsyncFunction declaring at least the path it
operates on. Measured on Deno the two regressions are gone.

The new fs/promises tests pin the arity table, the AsyncFunction/name contract
for everything use-m rebuilds, `watch` being the runtime's promise watcher
rather than the callback `fs.watch`, and an end-to-end round trip through the
rebuilt wrappers.
docs(case-study): record the passing CI run for the dynamic built-in change

feat(builtins): discover built-in modules at runtime

The hardcoded `supportedBuiltins` table answered two unrelated questions
with one map: how to polyfill a module in a browser, and how to import it
on the Node.js side. The second answer was the same one-liner 25 times
over — `import('node:<name>')` — while every built-in missing from the
table silently fell through to the npm and CDN resolvers. Measured on
Node.js 24.21.0, the built-in resolver claimed 24 of 72 built-ins; `tty`,
`cluster`, `worker_threads`, `vm`, `readline`, `string_decoder`,
`node:sqlite` and 41 others were treated as package names.

The supported set is now read from the runtime through `node:module`
(`isBuiltin`, falling back to `builtinModules`), so it claims 72 of 72 and
covers built-ins added after this release. Only the cases the language
cannot derive are kept: browser polyfills for `console`, `crypto`, `url`
and `performance`, the `performance` -> `node:perf_hooks` mapping, and a
`fs/promises` rebuild for Bun and Deno, whose promise functions report the
wrong arity and constructor. Even there the function list and arities come
from the runtime instead of being written down.

Each entry file loses 114 lines (-5.5% raw). Resolves #50.

commit.message:
test: pin command-stream integration version

Registry latest moved from 0.0.5 to an incompatible 0.19.0, making the resolver integration assertions depend on release timing.

fix(npm): preserve aliases with shared binaries

Retry with force and disabled bin linking only after the conflicting symlink is verified to belong to another versioned alias of the same package. Unrelated executables remain untouched.
